# Interest-bearing loans, pledges and limits on debt bondage (`interest_loans_collateral`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/economy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Economy & finance (`economy`)
- Deps: helped by alphabet_writing, written_law_code, compound_interest_exponential_growth
- Core idea: A lender hands over grain, seed or silver for a fixed term and is paid back with an agreed extra (interest), under a written, witnessed contract secured by a pledge (land, goods) or a guarantor. Interest pays for waiting, for the risk of default and for what the lender gives up. Charitable and religious lenders also made interest-free loans. Mesopotamian law fixed customary maxima of 20 % a year on silver and 33⅓ % on barley. What keeps a credit system from wrecking society is a limit on what default can take: no enslavement of the debtor's person (or only for a short fixed time), a protected minimum of tools and land, and an orderly way to cancel unpayable debts (debt-release edicts, later bankruptcy law).
- Pitfalls:
  - Banning interest outright: lending goes underground or is disguised (bills of exchange, sale-and-buy-back, rent charges), and the hidden rate is higher because the risk is higher
  - Letting creditors seize the debtor's body or family: debt bondage built up until Solon had to cancel debts (594 BC) and Mesopotamian kings issued release edicts
  - Fixing a low legal maximum rate by decree: lenders simply stop lending to the poor
  - Forgetting compounding: a 33 % yearly debt left unpaid triples in under four years
  - Assuming medieval Christians or Muslims did no lending: bans changed the form of finance, not its existence
- History: mesopotamia: c. 2400 BC – Enmetena of Lagash proclaims a release of debts; temples and palaces lend barley and silver, alongside private lenders (how far temples dominated is debated); c. 1754 BC Hammurabi caps interest at 20 % on silver and 33⅓ % on grain and limits debt servitude to three years (§117); c. 1646 BC Ammi-saduqa's release edict; egypt: Ptolemaic law caps interest at 24 % a year; india: c. 2nd c. BC–2nd c. AD – the Laws of Manu (8.140) fix 1¼ % a month on secured loans as the fair rate, higher by caste and risk; greece: 594 BC – Solon cancels debts secured on persons and forbids loans on the body (seisachtheia); rome: c. 450 BC – Twelve Tables cap interest; 326 BC (traditional) lex Poetelia ends nexum bondage for debt; Justinian caps ordinary interest at 6 %; china: Han–Tang – written loan contracts with guarantors survive at Dunhuang and Turfan; 1069 Wang Anshi's 'green sprouts' state loans to farmers, attacked as forced lending; islamic: 7th c. – riba forbidden; trade-based credit (murabaha, deferred-price sale) and profit-sharing partnership finance develop instead; europe: 1179 and 1311 – church councils condemn usury; 1462 first Monte di Pietà (Perugia), cheap pawn loans to the poor; 1545 England permits interest up to 10 %
- Read:
  - Michael Hudson & Marc Van De Mieroop (eds.), Debt and Economic Renewal in the Ancient Near East (2002)
  - Sidney Homer & Richard Sylla, A History of Interest Rates (2005)
